items.prompt: In feature-flag terms, what is merging?
choices: Putting code into the shared history
Showing the feature to the users
Deleting an old code path
items.explanation: Merging is a git event about history. It says nothing by itself about what users see.

items.prompt: What does releasing a feature mean?
choices: Merging its pull request into main
Making its behavior reachable by users
Deleting its branch
items.explanation: Release is about exposure to users, which a flag controls separately from the merge.

items.prompt: With its flag off, merged code is:
choices: Absent from main until the flag turns on
Visible only to administrators of the product
In main but inactive for users
items.explanation: The code is integrated; its behavior is simply not reachable.

items.prompt: Without flags, why do teams often hold a branch open until the feature is done?
choices: Merging would also release unfinished work
Git forbids merging a branch before the feature is finished
Branches are cheaper to maintain than small commits on main
items.explanation: When merge equals release, nobody can merge half a feature.

items.prompt: Which action should become cheap and routine on a team that uses flags?
choices: Releasing to everyone at once
Merging small changes to main
Rewriting shared history
items.explanation: Because merging no longer exposes users, small frequent merges become safe.

items.prompt: What is the fastest way to undo a bad release on a flagged feature?
choices: Rewrite main's history
Wait for the next sprint
Flip the flag off
items.explanation: Releasing is a runtime decision, so reversing it is a config change, not a code change.

items.prompt: True or false: merging and releasing are always the same event.
choices: False, flags let them happen at different times
True, once it is merged the code is always live
items.explanation: That coupling is exactly what flags remove.

items.prompt: The nine-day checkout PR stayed open mainly because:
choices: Git was too slow to merge a branch that large
Merging would have released an untested flow
Reviewers were unavailable for most of those nine days
items.explanation: Merge and release were coupled, so the branch could not land until it was fully ready.

items.prompt: A half-built feature is merged behind a flag set to off. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The merge released it to a small group, and the flag only widens that group later
Merged, not released; the real risk is deferred to the moment the flag is flipped
It is not really part of main until the flag has been switched on for users
Deploys are now unsafe, since unfinished code is present in the shared history
items.explanation: Merge integrates code; release exposes behavior. The flag flip is now the risky decision, and it can be staged and reversed.
items.reference:
Merge is not release
🔀 Merge: code enters the shared history
🚦 Release: users can reach the behavior
🎚️ A flag puts a gap between the two
Why: a flag lets code be merged long before it is released, so each step carries its own, smaller risk.
items.learnMore:
Two events that used to be one

Without a flag, reaching main means reaching customers, so teams hold work back until it is finished. With a flag, merging becomes routine and releasing becomes a deliberate, staged decision.

Common mistake

Assuming code that is merged behind a flag is automatically safe. It still has to leave the old path untouched while the flag is off.
items.reflection: A restaurant can prep a new dish in the kitchen for days before it appears on the menu. What is the equivalent of the menu in other work you do?

items.prompt: Which situation shows merge and release being coupled?
choices: A developer merges small changes every day, each one hidden behind a flag
A finished but risky change sits unmerged for weeks because landing it would expose every user
A reviewer approves a pull request within an hour of it being opened
A kill switch is flipped by on-call during an incident to stop errors
items.explanation: When landing equals exposing, risky work is held back and its branch drifts, which is the nine-day PR pattern.

items.prompt: After a team adopts flags, where does the risky decision move?
choices: From the deploy step over to the code review step of the pipeline
From the merge to the moment a flag is turned up for users
From the testing phase over to the early design phase of the feature
Nowhere at all, the team only gets new vocabulary for the same decision
items.explanation: Merging becomes low-stakes, and the high-stakes choice becomes how widely and how fast to turn the flag up.

items.prompt: Which flag hides an unfinished feature until it is ready?
choices: Permission toggle
Experiment flag
Release toggle
items.explanation: Release toggles keep in-progress work off while it merges.

items.prompt: Which flag lets on-call disable a risky path without a deploy?
choices: Release toggle
Ops toggle (kill switch)
Experiment flag
Permission toggle
items.explanation: A kill switch exists for fast, deploy-free shutdown during incidents.

items.prompt: Which flag splits users to measure which variant performs better?
choices: Release toggle
Experiment flag
Kill switch
items.explanation: Experiment flags route groups of users to variants to compare results.

items.prompt: Which flag gives paid plans a feature free plans lack?
choices: Release toggle
Experiment flag
Permission toggle
items.explanation: Permission toggles encode who is allowed to use something.

items.prompt: Which kind should be removed soon after its feature fully ships?
choices: Release toggle
Permission toggle
Kill switch
items.explanation: Once the feature is at 100 percent and stable, the flag and the old path are dead weight.

items.prompt: Which kind is most likely to be kept for years on purpose?
choices: Release toggle
Permission toggle
Experiment flag
items.explanation: Plan gating is an ongoing business rule, not a temporary rollout.

items.prompt: A flag sends 50 percent of visitors to a new layout to compare signups. It is a:
choices: Kill switch
Permission toggle
Experiment flag
items.explanation: Splitting traffic to measure an outcome is an experiment.

items.prompt: A switch that turns off recommendations when that service is overloaded is a:
choices: Release toggle
Experiment flag
Permission toggle
Kill switch
items.explanation: It protects the system during trouble and stays available as a safety net.

items.prompt: Flag new-search has served 100 percent of users for a year. Which kind of flag has this team mishandled?
choices: A permission toggle that was kept on purpose
A release toggle left in place after rollout
A kill switch doing its job
An experiment that is still running
items.explanation: A release toggle's job ends at full rollout; leaving it adds a dead code path with no benefit.
items.reference:
Four kinds of flag
🚧 Release: hide unfinished work, delete soon
🛑 Ops / kill switch: disable a risky path fast, keep
🧪 Experiment: split users to measure, delete after
🔑 Permission: gate by plan or role, often permanent
Why: the kind of flag determines how long it should live, and only release and experiment flags should be deleted.
items.learnMore:
Purpose sets lifetime

All four kinds are the same mechanism, a runtime check, but they answer different questions. Release and experiment flags are temporary by design. Kill switches and permission toggles are intentionally long-lived.

Common mistake

Using one kind for another's job, such as a release toggle for plan gating, which then gets deleted as stale cleanup.
items.reflection: A building has a fire door that stays installed forever and scaffolding that comes down when the work ends. Which of your own tools or habits are scaffolding, and which are fire doors?

items.prompt: Which flag should survive after its feature is fully rolled out?
choices: A release toggle for a new button
An experiment flag whose test concluded
A kill switch guarding an expensive dependency
A flag for a one-off migration
items.explanation: Kill switches are meant to remain as a fast off button; release and experiment flags are scaffolding.

items.prompt: How does an experiment flag differ from a release toggle?
choices: It keeps users deliberately split to measure an outcome, rather than moving toward 100 percent
It cannot be changed at runtime because its split is compiled in at build time
It is always permanent and has to stay in the code forever once created
It only ever applies to internal users and never to real customers
items.explanation: A release toggle is a temporary path to everyone; an experiment holds a split on purpose until it has a verdict.

items.prompt: Someone proposes a release toggle to gate a feature to the paid tier. What goes wrong?
choices: Paid users cannot see release toggles, so the gate would simply not work
Release toggles are technically unable to target a user's plan tier
It makes every deploy noticeably slower for the whole team to ship
It is permanent business logic that will be mistaken for stale cleanup and removed
items.explanation: Plan gating should be modelled as a permission toggle with a long-lived owner, so cleanup sweeps leave it alone.

items.prompt: Where does the not-yet-ready version of a flagged feature live?
choices: In a long-lived branch
In main, behind a runtime check
On the developer's laptop
items.explanation: The flag keeps it integrated and inactive.

items.prompt: With flags, the old and new paths sit in:
choices: Separate histories merged later
Different repositories
The same history
items.explanation: One line of history holds both; a runtime decision chooses.

items.prompt: The basic shape of a flag check is:
choices: An if/else choosing old or new behavior
A git hook
A database migration
items.explanation: It is a conditional at the point where behavior diverges.

items.prompt: What should a brand-new feature's flag default to?
choices: On
Off
Random
items.explanation: Default off means a deploy changes nothing until someone decides to release.

items.prompt: With flags, which step is the risky one?
choices: Merging a small, reviewed pull request to main
Deploying a build in which the flag is still off
Turning the flag up for real users
items.explanation: Exposure is where users can be affected.

items.prompt: Can the old and new flows be deployed at the same time?
choices: No, only one can be in main
Yes, the flag chooses at runtime
items.explanation: Both are in the build; the flag decides per request.

items.prompt: Why can a team merge half a feature safely?
choices: Git hides the unmerged half from the other developers
The unfinished half is unreachable while the flag is off
Reviewers are allowed to skip code that is not enabled
items.explanation: Unreachable code cannot affect users.

items.prompt: Who decides which path a request takes?
choices: The name of the current git branch
The CI server that built the release
The flag evaluation at runtime
items.explanation: The check runs on each request using current config.

items.prompt: A half-built feature is merged behind a flag. What is the most important thing to test before merging?
choices: With the flag off, existing behavior is unchanged
The new path is already free of bugs and ready for all customers
The flag has already been switched on in production for real users
The branch name follows the naming convention the team agreed on
items.explanation: While the flag is off, the old path is all users see, so it must be untouched.
items.reference:
One history, two paths
🧭 A runtime check picks old or new
📚 Both paths live in main, in small PRs
🎚️ Default off, flip later
Why: the unfinished version lives in the code behind a check, not in a divergent git branch.
items.learnMore:
Branching in code instead of in git

Instead of two histories that must be reconciled later, there is one history containing both paths and a decision that chooses between them at runtime. Deploying is routine; flipping the flag is the careful step.

Common mistake

Spreading the flag check across many shared helpers, so unrelated callers change behavior and the flag becomes hard to remove.
items.reflection: A road with a closed lane behind cones lets work proceed without redirecting all traffic. Where else do you keep two options available and pick one at the last moment?

items.prompt: A PR puts the flag check inside a helper used by ten callers rather than at the checkout entry point. What is the main risk?
choices: Git cannot merge a shared helper that has a flag inside it
Unrelated callers may take the new path, widening the blast radius
The flag can never be deleted, even after a complete rollout
The helper becomes faster because it now runs only one of the paths
items.explanation: A check should sit at the narrowest point where behavior diverges, or the flag affects more than intended.

Both paths are identical, so there is nothing left that can conflict

items.prompt: What does a flag's default decide?
choices: The value for anyone no rule matches
The first rule to run
Whether the kill switch is on
items.explanation: Default is the fallback after all rules.

items.prompt: How are targeting rules evaluated?
choices: All at once, majority wins
In order, first match wins
Randomly
items.explanation: Evaluation stops at the first rule that matches.

items.prompt: Which rule type serves specific accounts such as QA staff?
choices: A percentage rollout
The default
A user id list
items.explanation: A list targets named users directly.

items.prompt: A 0 percent rollout gives the new path to:
choices: Nobody
Everyone
Only staff
items.explanation: Zero percent selects no buckets.

items.prompt: What does widening a rollout from 5 to 25 percent require?
choices: A brand new deploy of the application
Only a config change
A new branch created off main
items.explanation: The audience is data, not code.

items.prompt: Which audience usually comes first in a staged rollout?
choices: All customers
Enterprise accounts
Internal or QA users
items.explanation: Staff catch obvious bugs before any customer is exposed.

items.prompt: Why not just use on/off for everything?
choices: It forces an all-or-nothing release
An on/off switch is slower to evaluate
Flags are not allowed to be boolean values
items.explanation: Without targeting, the release is as risky as the giant PR.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT a targeting rule input?
choices: The user id of the person making the request
The git commit hash of the feature
The plan tier of the account making the request
items.explanation: Rules use runtime facts about the user or request.

items.prompt: Rules in order: (1) user in QA list serves on, (2) plan enterprise serves off, (3) 5 percent rollout serves on, default off. A QA user on the enterprise plan sees:
choices: On
Off
Depends on their bucket
An error
items.explanation: Rule 1 matches first, so evaluation stops there.
items.reference:
Ordered rules, first match wins
1️⃣ Rules are checked top to bottom
✅ The first matching rule decides
⬇️ No match: the default applies
Why: order is part of a flag's meaning, so a broad rule above a narrow one can make the narrow one unreachable.
items.learnMore:
A flag is a small ordered program

Targeting rules let one deployed build serve different people differently: staff first, then a slice of users, with exclusions and a default. Reordering rules changes outcomes without any code change.

Common mistake

Placing an exclusion below a broader rule and assuming it still applies to everyone it names.
items.reflection: Airport boarding calls groups in order, and your group is the first one that fits you. How would the result change if the groups were called in a different order?

items.prompt: Same rules. A non-QA enterprise user whose bucket is 2 sees:
choices: On
Depends on the deploy
Off
The default of on
items.explanation: Rule 2 matches before the rollout rule is reached.

items.prompt: Which mistake makes an exclusion silently fail?
choices: Setting the default to off instead of leaving it undefined in the config
Writing the rules in a config file rather than hardcoding them
Using more than two rules in the same flag configuration

items.prompt: A well-built percentage rollout is sticky per:
choices: Request
Server
User
items.explanation: Each user should get the same answer every time.

items.prompt: What is hashed to place a user in a bucket?
choices: A stable id plus the flag key
The current timestamp of the request
A random number drawn on each request
items.explanation: Only stable inputs give repeatable results.

items.prompt: Hashing the same input twice gives:
choices: Different outputs
The same output
An error
items.explanation: Determinism is what makes bucketing sticky.

items.prompt: With 100 buckets, a user in bucket 3 and a 5 percent rollout gets:
choices: The old path
An error
The new path
items.explanation: Buckets 0 to 4 are inside 5 percent.

items.prompt: When the rollout widens from 5 to 25 percent, users who already had the feature:
choices: Keep it
Lose it
Are reshuffled
items.explanation: Their bucket is still below the larger percent.

items.prompt: Why avoid a random choice per request?
choices: It is too slow to run on every request
A user could flip between versions mid-flow
Hashing a user id is not allowed by law
items.explanation: Checkout spans several requests that must agree.

items.prompt: Roughly how many of 10,000 users are in a 5 percent rollout?
choices: About 50
About 5,000
About 500
items.explanation: 5 percent of 10,000 is 500, give or take normal variation.

items.prompt: Why include the flag key in the hash?
choices: So each flag selects users independently
To make the hashing step run faster
To hide the user id from the logs
items.explanation: Otherwise the same users would be early adopters of every flag.

items.prompt: A user is in bucket 12. The rollout goes 10, then 20, then 5 percent. At which stages do they see the feature?
choices: Yes, yes, yes
No, yes, no
No, no, no
Yes, yes, no
items.explanation: They see it only when 12 is below the percent: not at 10, yes at 20, not at 5.
items.reference:
Same user, same answer
🔑 Hash user id plus flag key
🪣 Bucket 0-99
📏 Bucket below percent: new path
Why: deriving the decision from stable inputs makes each user's answer repeatable, and nests smaller rollouts inside larger ones.
items.learnMore:
Percent of users, not percent of requests

A hash turns a stable id into a fixed bucket. The same user always lands in the same bucket, so refreshes do not flip them, and raising the percentage only adds users. Mixing the flag key into the hash decorrelates different flags.

Common mistake

Rolling a random number per request, which gives 5 percent of requests and lets one user see both versions.
items.reflection: A school assigns each student a locker number from their name, so it is always the same. Where in your own work would a stable assignment beat a fresh random choice?

items.prompt: Two flags both roll out to 5 percent, but both hash only the user id. What happens?

Nobody gets either flag
The same users get every flag first
Rollouts become 10 percent
items.explanation: Identical hashing means identical buckets, so the same people are always chosen.

Which setting caps how many users can meet a bug?

The commit message
The rollout percentage
items.explanation: Exposure is bounded by who is in the rollout.

items.prompt: What does a kill switch do?
choices: Turns the path off for everyone without a deploy
Deletes the new code from main
Rolls back the database to its earlier state
items.explanation: It flips behavior at runtime.

items.prompt: Gradual widening turns 'a bug for everyone' into:
choices: No bugs at all in the new path
A bug for a known, bounded slice
A bug that nobody is able to find
items.explanation: It does not prevent bugs, it limits their reach.

items.prompt: Damage from a bug is roughly exposure multiplied by:
choices: Number of files changed
Team size
Time until it is detected
items.explanation: More people for longer means more harm.

items.prompt: 25 percent of 40,000 users is:
A bug caught at 5 percent instead of 100 percent reaches how many times fewer users?
choices: 5 times fewer
20 times fewer
100 times fewer
items.explanation: 100 divided by 5 is 20.

items.prompt: Which recovers faster from a bad flagged release?
choices: Revert and redeploy
Flip the kill switch
items.explanation: No build or deploy is in the way of a config flip.

items.prompt: A defect ships to 20,000 users. How many are exposed if it is caught at 5 percent versus at 100 percent?
choices: 100 versus 2,000
items.explanation: Exposure is percent times users: 0.05 times 20,000 is 1,000.
items.reference:
Exposure is a dial
📊 Exposed = percent × users
⏱️ Damage ≈ exposure × time to detect
🛑 Kill switch shortens time, staging shrinks exposure
Why: staging limits how many people a bug reaches and the kill switch limits how long it lasts, and you want both.
items.learnMore:
Two levers on the cost of a bug

Gradual widening bounds how many users meet a defect before someone notices. The kill switch bounds how long it lives. Neither reverses data already written by the new path.

Common mistake

Believing a kill switch alone makes a full-speed rollout safe. It reduces duration, not the number of people exposed in the meantime.
items.reflection: A new recipe is tried on one table before the whole dining room. What small, reversible trial could you run before a bigger change in your own work?

items.prompt: The kill switch is flipped, but the new path already wrote records in a new format. What is still true?
choices: The behavior is reversed, but the data already written remains
Everything is reverted automatically, data included, when the flag goes off
The records the new path wrote are deleted by the flag system
The flag can never be turned back on after a kill switch was used
items.explanation: A flag changes which code runs, not what that code already stored.

items.prompt: Why stage 5, 25, 100 percent instead of jumping to 100 with a kill switch standing by?
choices: Staging makes the kill switch unnecessary, since bugs cannot get through
Jumping to 100 is easier to monitor because every user is exposed at once
Percentages are required by Git for any change that touches production
Staging limits how many people are exposed during detection delay; the kill switch only limits duration
items.explanation: Detection is never instant, so exposure at the moment of detection is what staging controls.

items.prompt: During a rollout you compare errors for flag-on users against flag-off users at the same time. Why is that better than comparing to yesterday?
choices: It needs less data and so can be done by hand without any tooling
It avoids hashing, which is otherwise too slow to run on every request
It controls for traffic and other changes that vary over time
Yesterday's data is always wrong because systems change every single day
items.explanation: A concurrent comparison group shares the same conditions, so the difference points at the flag.

items.prompt: What is the last stage of a release toggle's life?
choices: Delete the flag and the old path
Raise its rollout up to 200 percent
Rename it
items.explanation: Cleanup is what turns scaffolding back into simple code.

items.prompt: A flag stuck at 100 percent for months is:
choices: A safety net
Debt
A requirement
items.explanation: It adds a branch to read with no remaining benefit.

items.prompt: How many combinations do 2 independent flags allow?
items.explanation: Each flag doubles the count: 2 times 2.

items.prompt: How many combinations do 3 independent flags allow?
items.explanation: 2 to the power of 3.

items.prompt: Cleanup of a release toggle should be part of:
choices: A someday backlog of cleanup tickets
The feature's definition of done
The next hiring round for the team
items.explanation: If it is optional it tends not to happen.

items.prompt: Which flag kind is kept on purpose after rollouts finish?
choices: A release toggle
A concluded experiment
A kill switch
items.explanation: It is the standing safety net.

items.prompt: After full rollout, the old code path is:
choices: Dead code that readers must still understand
Required by the new path to keep working
Faster than the new path in every case
items.explanation: Nothing uses it, but it still has to be read and avoided.

items.prompt: Each active flag adds:
choices: A new repository for each flag
Another independent code path
A new server for each flag
items.explanation: It is an extra fork in behavior.

items.prompt: Ten independent flags are active. What is the upper bound on distinct path combinations?
items.explanation: 2 to the power of 10 is 1,024.
items.reference:
Why flags must die
🌱 Created: default off
📈 Partial then full rollout
🧹 Delete flag and old path
✖️ n flags: up to 2^n combinations
Why: a flag at 100 percent no longer reduces risk, but it still multiplies the paths every change must consider.
items.learnMore:
Flag debt

Each active flag is an independent fork, so interacting flags push the number of combinations toward 2 to the n. Deleting finished release toggles keeps that number small. Treat removal as part of the feature's definition of done.

Common mistake

Leaving cleanup as a follow-up ticket with no owner. It rarely gets prioritized.
items.reflection: Temporary shortcuts in a kitchen, a garage or a codebase tend to become permanent unless someone owns taking them out. What temporary thing in your life has no removal date?

items.prompt: A team has 40 flags, 25 of them at 100 percent for over six months. Best first move?
choices: Add a dashboard that lists every flag and its owner for the team
Raise the remaining 15 flags to 100 percent as quickly as possible
Delete the fully rolled out release toggles and their dead paths
Freeze all merges until someone has reviewed every flag by hand
items.explanation: Removing finished toggles cuts the combination count the fastest without losing any safety.

items.prompt: Why is 2 to the n an upper bound rather than the real count of paths?
choices: Flags can only ever be on, so half of the combinations never exist
Many flags guard unrelated code, so not every combination can interact
Git limits the number of flags a repository can hold to n
Hashing removes combinations by sending each user to a single bucket
items.explanation: Reachability and interaction limit how many combinations actually matter, but interacting flags approach the bound.

items.prompt: Which practice best stops stale flags piling up?
choices: A rule that new flags cannot be created without manager approval
A yearly cleanup week where everyone deletes whatever flags they remember
Leaving flags in the code forever so nobody has to decide anything
A removal task with an owner and expiry created together with the flag
items.explanation: Ownership and a date at creation make removal part of the work, not an afterthought.

items.prompt: Implement `flagFor(config, userId)`. `config` has a boolean `default` and an array `userIds`. Return `true` if `userIds` contains `userId`, otherwise return `config.default`.

tests.expr: expect(flagFor({ default: false, userIds: ["a"] }, "a")).toBe(true)
expect(flagFor({ default: false, userIds: ["a"] }, "b")).toBe(false)
expect(flagFor({ default: true, userIds: [] }, "z")).toBe(true)

items.explanation: A targeted match wins; everyone else falls through to the default.

items.prompt: Implement `isOn(config, userId)`. If `config.killSwitch` is true, return `false` no matter what. Otherwise return `true` if `config.userIds` contains `userId`, else `config.default`.

tests.description: kill switch overrides a listed user
tests.expr: expect(isOn({ killSwitch: true, default: true, userIds: ["a"] }, "a")).toBe(false)

tests.description: listed user is on when kill switch is off
tests.expr: expect(isOn({ killSwitch: false, default: false, userIds: ["a"] }, "a")).toBe(true)
expect(isOn({ killSwitch: false, default: true, userIds: [] }, "q")).toBe(true)

items.explanation: The kill switch is checked first so nothing below it can keep the path alive.

items.prompt: Implement `firstMatch(rules, userId, fallback)`. `rules` is an array of `{ userIds, serve }`. Return `serve` from the first rule whose `userIds` contains `userId`. If none match, return `fallback`.

tests.expr: expect(firstMatch([{ userIds: ["a"], serve: true }, { userIds: ["a"], serve: false }], "a", false)).toBe(true)

tests.description: later rule matches when earlier does not
tests.expr: expect(firstMatch([{ userIds: ["x"], serve: true }, { userIds: ["a"], serve: false }], "a", true)).toBe(false)
expect(firstMatch([{ userIds: ["x"], serve: true }], "a", false)).toBe(false)

items.explanation: Returning inside the loop stops at the first match, which is exactly first-match-wins.

items.prompt: Implement `inRollout(bucket, percent)`. A user with a bucket from 0 to 99 is in the rollout when `bucket` is strictly less than `percent`. Return a boolean.

tests.expr: expect(inRollout(3, 5)).toBe(true)

tests.description: bucket equal to percent is out
tests.expr: expect(inRollout(5, 5)).toBe(false)
expect(inRollout(0, 0)).toBe(false)
expect(inRollout(99, 100)).toBe(true)

items.explanation: Strictly-less-than makes 0 percent empty and 100 percent complete, and widening the percent only ever adds buckets.

items.prompt: Implement `evaluate(config, ctx)` returning `{ enabled, reason }` (in that key order). If `config.killSwitch` is true return `{ enabled: false, reason: "kill-switch" }`. Otherwise walk `config.rules` in order: a rule of `type` `"userIdIn"` matches when `rule.values` includes `ctx.userId`; a rule of type `"planTier"` matches when `rule.values` includes `ctx.planTier`. The first match returns `{ enabled: rule.serve, reason: rule.type }`. If nothing matches return `{ enabled: config.default, reason: "default" }`.

tests.description: kill switch wins over a matching rule
tests.expr: expect(evaluate({ killSwitch: true, default: true, rules: [{ type: "userIdIn", values: ["a"], serve: true }] }, { userId: "a", planTier: "free" })).toEqual({ enabled: false, reason: "kill-switch" })
expect(evaluate({ killSwitch: false, default: false, rules: [{ type: "userIdIn", values: ["a"], serve: true }] }, { userId: "a", planTier: "free" })).toEqual({ enabled: true, reason: "userIdIn" })

const rules = [{ type: "planTier", values: ["enterprise"], serve: false }, { type: "userIdIn", values: ["a"], serve: true }]; expect(evaluate({ killSwitch: false, default: true, rules }, { userId: "a", planTier: "enterprise" })).toEqual({ enabled: false, reason: "planTier" })
expect(evaluate({ killSwitch: false, default: true, rules: [{ type: "userIdIn", values: ["x"], serve: false }] }, { userId: "a", planTier: "free" })).toEqual({ enabled: true, reason: "default" })
expect(evaluate({ killSwitch: false, default: false, rules: [] }, { userId: "a", planTier: "free" })).toEqual({ enabled: false, reason: "default" })

items.explanation: The kill switch is an early return before any rule runs. Inside the loop, returning on the first match gives first-match-wins, and the reason records which rule decided. Only after the loop does the default apply.
items.reference:
Precedence of a flag decision
🛑 Kill switch beats everything
1️⃣ Rules: top to bottom, first match wins
⬇️ No match: the default
🏷️ Return the reason with the answer
Why: a fixed order of checks is what makes a flag's behavior predictable and explainable.
items.learnMore:
Rules as an ordered program

The evaluator checks the kill switch, then walks the rules in order and stops at the first match, otherwise it serves the default. Returning the reason makes every decision explainable after the fact.

Common mistake

Continuing past a match or checking the kill switch last, so a broken path can stay alive during an incident.
items.reflection: A bouncer checks a ban list first, then the guest list, then applies the house rule. Where else do you apply checks in a strict order, and what breaks if the order changes?

items.prompt: Implement `evaluateRollout(config, ctx)` returning `{ enabled, reason }` (in that key order). Kill switch first: `{ enabled: false, reason: "kill-switch" }`. Then walk `config.rules` in order. A rule of type `"userIdIn"` matches when `rule.values` includes `ctx.userId`. A rule of type `"percentageRollout"` matches when `ctx.bucket` (a number 0 to 99, already computed) is strictly less than `rule.percent`. The first match returns `{ enabled: rule.serve, reason: rule.type }`; otherwise `{ enabled: config.default, reason: "default" }`.

tests.description: bucket inside the percent is enabled
tests.expr: expect(evaluateRollout({ killSwitch: false, default: false, rules: [{ type: "percentageRollout", percent: 5, serve: true }] }, { userId: "u", bucket: 3 })).toEqual({ enabled: true, reason: "percentageRollout" })

tests.description: bucket outside the percent falls to default
tests.expr: expect(evaluateRollout({ killSwitch: false, default: false, rules: [{ type: "percentageRollout", percent: 5, serve: true }] }, { userId: "u", bucket: 5 })).toEqual({ enabled: false, reason: "default" })

tests.description: widening the percent keeps an already-included user
tests.expr: const mk = (p) => ({ killSwitch: false, default: false, rules: [{ type: "percentageRollout", percent: p, serve: true }] }); expect(evaluateRollout(mk(5), { userId: "u", bucket: 3 }).enabled).toBe(true); expect(evaluateRollout(mk(25), { userId: "u", bucket: 3 }).enabled).toBe(true)

tests.description: an earlier userIdIn rule beats the rollout
tests.expr: expect(evaluateRollout({ killSwitch: false, default: false, rules: [{ type: "userIdIn", values: ["qa"], serve: false }, { type: "percentageRollout", percent: 100, serve: true }] }, { userId: "qa", bucket: 0 })).toEqual({ enabled: false, reason: "userIdIn" })

tests.description: kill switch beats a full rollout
tests.expr: expect(evaluateRollout({ killSwitch: true, default: true, rules: [{ type: "percentageRollout", percent: 100, serve: true }] }, { userId: "u", bucket: 0 })).toEqual({ enabled: false, reason: "kill-switch" })

items.explanation: A rollout rule is just another ordered rule whose test is bucket below percent. Because the bucket is a stable input, a user included at 5 stays included at 25, and an earlier targeted rule still outranks the rollout.

items.prompt: Implement `insertBeforeRollout(rules, rule)`. Return a NEW array in which `rule` is inserted immediately before the first element whose `type` is `"percentageRollout"`. If there is no such element, append `rule` at the end. Do not modify the input array.

tests.expr: const r = [{ type: "userIdIn" }, { type: "percentageRollout" }]; expect(insertBeforeRollout(r, { type: "planTier" })).toEqual([{ type: "userIdIn" }, { type: "planTier" }, { type: "percentageRollout" }])

tests.description: appends when there is no rollout rule
tests.expr: expect(insertBeforeRollout([{ type: "userIdIn" }], { type: "planTier" })).toEqual([{ type: "userIdIn" }, { type: "planTier" }])
const r = [{ type: "percentageRollout" }]; insertBeforeRollout(r, { type: "planTier" }); expect(r).toEqual([{ type: "percentageRollout" }])
expect(insertBeforeRollout([], { type: "planTier" })).toEqual([{ type: "planTier" }])

items.explanation: Position is the only thing that changes a rule's priority, so the helper finds the rollout rule and splices ahead of it, using a copy so the live config is never edited in place.
